evidence.title: Uses of generative AI by non-clinician staff at an academic medical center
evidence.outcome: Off-label use of chat tool unrelated to work or organizational goals, including clinical decision-making queries
evidence.effect: A notable proportion of interactions were off-label queries unrelated to work or organizational goals, including 5.9% involving clinical decision-making.
evidence.quote: A notable proportion of interactions included off-label queries unrelated to work or organizational goals, including 5.9% involving clinical decision-making.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether periodic audits of AI use against intended use, or channels for reporting off-label use, reduce drift beyond validated scope. One deployment study found that 5.9% of 30,503 chat threads involved clinical decision-making queries outside the tool's intended purpose, which shows the hazard occurs in practice.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice. The single cross-sectional study from a U.S. deployment documents off-label use but does not compare audited and unaudited settings. Five sources endorse the practice, all frameworks or commentaries, and their agreement reflects expert consensus rather than measured effect. Certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In one deployment, 5.9% of chat threads involved clinical decision-making, a use the tool was not validated to support. Unvalidated clinical advice could reach patients through clinician decisions without any record of the tool's role. Whether audits detect such use early enough to prevent harm has not been studied.

The hazard study classified 30,503 chat threads by purpose, which suggests that log review can identify off-label queries in a live system. The study did not report the staff time, classification accuracy, or audit frequency needed to run such review as an ongoing governance task, so its feasibility as a routine control remains unmeasured.

The NIST Generative AI Profile calls for re-evaluating risk when models are adapted to new domains, and the CHAI guides call for intermittent audits of use against intended purpose. These sources frame off-label use as a trigger for reassessment. No study reports whether organizations following this guidance detect scope drift more often.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare sites that audit AI use against intended use with sites that do not, measuring how often off-label clinical use is detected, how quickly it is corrected, the staff time required, and any downstream effect on patient harm.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, and the hazard study did not report whether its setting included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so it is unknown whether off-label use or its detection differs in settings that serve these groups.
